properties.decision:
Recorded as BRAINSTORMING, not as a proposal — the detector leg of rule:a-reflow2-tool-failure-met-while-working-is-captured-as-a-to-do, which asks the AGENT to write down every tool failure it meets. The agent's idea, raised while recording the rule, 2026-09-06.

THE OBSERVATION: every refusal reflow2 issues passes through the server. The agent has to remember to record it; the server already knows. A rule that depends on the agent remembering is the failure mode the root-cause skill was written against ("a rule is read once and states an intention").

THE OPTIONS:
(a) A REFUSALS LEDGER IN THE DESIGN — the server appends a dated observation per refusal (tool, refusal class, masked message shape), on the capability the tool realizes, in the design being served. Then "where does reflow2 fail" is a scan, and the rule's compliance is checkable: a refusal the ledger holds with no defect fact or recurrence written by the session afterwards is the absence. Counter-argument: it writes into the USER's design on every refusal — dozens a session on a busy day — and a design that fills with reflow2's own bookkeeping is the wallpaper failure; and a refusal is often the loop working (a near-duplicate guard doing its job), which no ledger can tell from a defect.
(b) A COUNTER, NOT A LEDGER — per tool, per refusal class, counts only, surfaced by loop_status or a friction report, never as nodes. Cheap, no design pollution; dec:bl-155 already measured unused tools this way. Counter-argument: a count says WHERE, never WHY, and the reason is what the maintainer needs; it also reaches only the server's own view, not a workaround the agent took after a reply that was technically not a refusal (the export stamp case).
(c) TELEMETRY — refusal classes leave the machine as usage events (req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content: log the verb, never the object). Reaches the maintainer from every consumer's design, which is exactly Anthony's worry. Counter-argument: opt-in, absent today, and a refusal class without its context is a number in a dashboard.
(d) THE HOOK — PostToolUse on mcp__reflow2__.* already fires (reflow2_init.py registers it); it could inject "you were just refused by X — record it or say why not". One harness only (dec:idea-the-loop-nudge-exists-for-one-harness-only). Counter-argument: the same as the root-cause hook option — reaches one harness, teaches skimming if it fires on every guard.

A RANKING IS A FINDING: (b) is the cheapest honest floor and keeps the design clean; (a) is the only one that makes the rule's compliance computable in the design; (c) is the one that reaches other people's designs, which is the stated reason for the rule; (d) is free and partial. None built.
properties.name: OPEN — should the server record its own refusals (a refusals ledger per tool, kept in the design), so that "where does reflow2 fail" is computed rather than remembered, and a session that swallowed one can be noticed?
properties.no_relation_note: Searched the design for a refusals ledger, friction counting and tool-failure tracking; nearest were the manual-work reports (report_manual_work records what the agent did BY HAND, not what the server refused) and dec:bl-155 (unused-tool counts, which cannot tell unused from unreachable). Neither is the same question, so no relation was drawn; the rule this is the detector leg of is linked from the rule's own text and this node is distinct from it by type and by asking the mechanism rather than stating the practice.
properties.rationale: Raised beside the rule rather than left in the conversation because the rule's own text names it as owed: the rule is the instruction leg, the defect facts are the record leg, and nothing notices a refusal nobody wrote down. Whether any of it is worth building is Anthony's call; the cheapest measurement first would be (b) run for a week to see how many refusals a real session meets, since the wallpaper objection to (a) turns entirely on that number.
